**Title:** Same Name, Different Unit: Identifying Source-Specific Units in Web Price Fusion

**Abstract (269 words):**

Price services convert and fuse quotes across venues and units, and assume that every source's dollar is the same dollar. Often it is not: a crypto exchange's dollar balance is a claim on that exchange and can lose value when its banking fails, and a service then mistakes a change in the dollar for a change in price. We identify such a unit shift from public prices. What all assets on an exchange share in their price gaps measures its dollar offset, and a stablecoin traded there, corrected for its price elsewhere, separates a move in the dollar from demand for the assets. On Bitfinex from November 2018 to May 2019, net of Tether's own price on Kraken, its Tether price tracked the offset with slope 0.97 (95% interval 0.94 to 1.00); Binance.US in 2023 gave 1.00, close to mechanical. A pre-registered panel of eight currency units gave a pooled 0.978 (0.962 to 0.989), just short of its pre-registered target of an interval including one and partly reflecting triangular arbitrage within each venue, and a pre-registered Kraken slice, uninformative about a wedge, gave 1.005 (0.867 to 1.289). A plain median was hard to beat in three fusion tests and failed in two pre-registered ones. Where most trading shared a stablecoin that lost its peg, a frozen unit-aware method beat it (log-error difference −1.08, −1.36 to −0.83). In six local-currency markets, converting at official rates erred by 128.1 bps against 6.8 through the venue's own stablecoin (8.30 with the stablecoin taken at par), and the median of officially converted markets by 107.4 bps against 5.4. We tested only crypto exchanges.

**Suggested keywords:** exchange dollars; unit of account; truth discovery; price feeds and oracles; Web data quality; cryptocurrency markets; reproducibility
